title: TB preventive treatment (WHO)
subject: infectious-disease
setting: Outpatient, HIV clinic, TB contact tracing
summary: Rule out active TB, then offer preventive treatment to people with HIV, household contacts of pulmonary TB and other high-risk groups, using 3HP, 6H, 3HR, 1HP or 4R (CDC prefers the short rifamycin regimens), and 6 months of daily levofloxacin for contacts of MDR/RR-TB.

sections.title: Who should receive TPT (WHO 2024)
items: People with HIV (adults, adolescents, and children 12 months or older in high-transmission settings): give TPT once TB disease is unlikely, regardless of CD4 count, ART, pregnancy or previous TB treatment, even if infection testing is unavailable. Infants under 12 months with HIV: only if they are TB contacts.

Household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB: children under 5 years should receive TPT even without an infection test; contacts aged 5 years or more may be given TPT once TB disease is excluded.

Systematically test and treat people starting anti-TNF therapy, on dialysis, preparing for organ or haematological transplant, or with silicosis. Consider testing prisoners, health workers, immigrants from high-burden countries, homeless people and people who use drugs.

Infection testing: tuberculin skin test (TST), IGRA or a TB antigen-based skin test (TBST). A test is not required for people with HIV or child contacts, and lack of a test must never block TPT for them.
Previous TB treatment and pregnancy are not contraindications to TPT.

sections.title: Rule out TB disease first
items: Adults and adolescents with HIV: screen for current cough, fever, weight loss or night sweats; any symptom needs evaluation for TB. Chest X-ray, CRP above 5 mg/L or a molecular test may also be used to screen.
HIV-negative contacts aged 5 or more and other risk groups: no TB symptoms plus a normal chest X-ray rules out TB disease.
Child contacts under 15: screen for cough, fever or poor weight gain, and/or chest X-ray. Take particular care to exclude TB in malnourished infants.
Any symptom or abnormal X-ray: investigate (sputum rapid molecular test, culture) and do not start TPT until TB disease is excluded.
Caution or defer: acute or chronic active hepatitis, transaminases above 3 times normal, regular heavy alcohol use, peripheral neuropathy (isoniazid). Do not give TPT in end-stage liver disease.

sections.title: Regimens for drug-susceptible exposure
items: WHO recommended options (any HIV status): 6 months of daily isoniazid (6H, or 9H); 3 months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid (3HP, 12 doses); 3 months of daily rifampicin plus isoniazid (3HR, 84 doses).
WHO alternatives: 1 month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid (1HP, 28 doses, age 13 or more) or 4 months of daily rifampicin (4R, 120 doses).
CDC/NTCA 2020 prefer the short rifamycin regimens (3HP, 4R, 3HR) over 6H or 9H because of better completion and less hepatotoxicity.

Adults 50 kg or more: 3HP isoniazid 900 mg plus rifapentine 900 mg once weekly; 1HP isoniazid 300 mg plus rifapentine 600 mg daily; 6H isoniazid 300 mg daily; 4R rifampicin 600 mg daily. See drug list for weight bands and children.
Children: 3HR with dispersible RH 75/50 mg is child-friendly; 3HP can be used at all ages with dispersible rifapentine and isoniazid by WHO weight band.

Rifapentine (3HP, 1HP): contraindicated with protease inhibitors, nevirapine, doravirine, etravirine and tenofovir alafenamide; usable with tenofovir disoproxil, efavirenz, dolutegravir and raltegravir. Rifampicin (3HR, 4R) needs dolutegravir or raltegravir dose adjustment.
Pyridoxine with isoniazid for those at risk of neuropathy, and routinely in pregnancy, breastfeeding and infants.

sections.title: Contacts of drug-resistant TB
items: Contacts of MDR/RR-TB: 6 months of daily levofloxacin (6Lfx) after TB disease is carefully excluded; infection testing is not required for children and people with HIV.
Contacts of isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible TB: 4R. Contacts of RR-TB whose index strain is isoniazid-susceptible may receive isoniazid.
If the index strain is fluoroquinolone-resistant, seek expert advice; moxifloxacin may replace levofloxacin only when levofloxacin is unavailable.
Pregnancy: discuss the risks and benefits of 6Lfx against deferring TPT to after delivery; levofloxacin can continue during breastfeeding.

sections.title: Monitoring, interruptions and completion
items: Review at each dispensing or monthly: adherence, TB symptoms and adverse effects (hepatitis, rash, neuropathy, flu-like or hypersensitivity reactions with 3HP). Stop and review for jaundice, dark urine, vomiting or abdominal pain.
Baseline liver tests are not routine; do them (and repeat during treatment if abnormal) for liver disease, regular alcohol use, HIV, age 35 or more, pregnancy or within 3 months of delivery.

Daily regimens (6H, 3HR, 4R, 6Lfx) interrupted under 2 weeks: resume and add the missed days. 2 weeks or more: continue if 80% or more of doses were taken, or if the course can still finish within the planned duration plus one third; otherwise restart, preferably with a shorter regimen.

3HP: a missed dose remembered within 2 days is taken and the schedule kept; later, take it and move the weekly day so doses stay at least 4 days apart. If 9 doses were taken within 12 weeks, complete within 112 days; 4 or more missed doses, restart or switch to a daily regimen.
1HP: up to 7 missed doses, complete the course within 42 days of starting; more than 7 consecutive missed doses, restart.

sections.title: Special groups
items: Pregnancy: 6H and 3HR are safe; rifapentine regimens (3HP, 1HP) are cautioned because of limited data. Give pyridoxine with isoniazid. Routine deferral of TPT to after delivery is not needed.
Well newborn of a mother with infectious TB: give TPT, delay BCG until 2 weeks after TPT ends, give pyridoxine 5 to 10 mg daily and continue breastfeeding.
Rifampicin and rifapentine reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy: advise barrier methods or an intrauterine device.
Hepatitis C on direct-acting antivirals: avoid rifamycin-based TPT (interaction).
India: NTEP uses similar regimens but tests contacts aged 5 or more for infection where possible and doses 6Lfx at 750 mg below 45 kg and 1 g at 45 kg or more; follow NTEP where it applies.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving single-drug TPT to someone with undiagnosed active TB, which selects resistance.
Withholding TPT from people with HIV or child contacts because TST, IGRA or X-ray is unavailable.
Starting rifamycin regimens with protease inhibitors, nevirapine or tenofovir alafenamide, or without contraceptive advice.
Using isoniazid or rifamycin regimens for contacts of MDR-TB, ignoring the index strain's resistance pattern.

drugs.name: 3HP: isoniazid plus rifapentine weekly
drugs.dose: Once weekly for 12 doses. 50 kg or more: isoniazid 900 mg plus rifapentine 900 mg (3 FDC 300/300 mg tablets). WHO 2024 bands: 10 to 14.9 kg H 250 mg + P 300 mg; 15 to 19.9 kg H 300 mg + P 450 mg; 20 to 29.9 kg H 450 mg + P 600 mg; 30 to 34.9 kg H 600 mg + P 750 mg; 35 to 39.9 kg H 600 mg + P 900 mg; 40 to 49.9 kg H 750 mg + P 900 mg
drugs.notes: Under 10 kg: WHO dispersible table. Flu-like and hypersensitivity reactions; supported or observed doses.

drugs.name: 1HP: isoniazid plus rifapentine daily
drugs.dose: Age 13 years or more: isoniazid 300 mg plus rifapentine 600 mg orally once daily for 28 days

drugs.name: Isoniazid (6H)
drugs.dose: Adults 5 mg/kg once daily, usually 300 mg (WHO 2024 bands: 30 to 64.9 kg 300 mg; 65 kg or more 375 mg). Children 10 mg/kg (7 to 15 mg/kg), maximum 300 mg. For 6 months (182 doses)
drugs.notes: Safe in pregnancy; add pyridoxine if at risk of neuropathy.

drugs.name: 3HR: rifampicin plus isoniazid daily
drugs.dose: Children: RH 75/50 mg dispersible, 4 to 7.9 kg 1 tablet, 8 to 11.9 kg 2, 12 to 15.9 kg 3, 16 to 24.9 kg 4. 25 kg or more: RH 150/75 mg, 25 to 29.9 kg 2 tablets, 30 to 34.9 kg 3, 35 to 64.9 kg 4, 65 kg or more 5. Daily for 3 months (84 doses)
drugs.notes: In adults hepatotoxicity is similar to 6H; 3HP may be preferred.

drugs.name: Rifampicin (4R)
drugs.dose: Adults 10 mg/kg once daily (WHO 2024 bands: 35 to 64.9 kg 600 mg; 65 kg or more 750 mg); children 15 mg/kg (10 to 20 mg/kg). For 4 months (120 doses)
drugs.notes: Also for contacts of isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible TB. Not practical under 25 kg (no child formulation).

drugs.name: Levofloxacin (6Lfx)
drugs.dose: 25 to 49.9 kg 500 mg; 50 kg or more 750 mg orally once daily for 6 months (WHO 2024). Smaller children: WHO weight-band table (dispersible 100 mg tablets)
drugs.notes: Contacts of MDR/RR-TB. Tendinopathy, QT prolongation, dysglycaemia.

drugs.name: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
drugs.dose: 10 to 25 mg orally daily with isoniazid; infants 5 to 10 mg daily; established neuropathy 50 to 75 mg daily (up to 100 to 200 mg)
drugs.notes: Routinely in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and for undernutrition, HIV, alcohol use, diabetes and CKD.
